solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: A flower to see in France? I’m going there (2,6)

indicatorNotes.in France: tells you to put 'to see' into French

blocks.note: a flower is something that flows, a river; the Ure is a Yorkshire river

annotation.surface: A tourist planning to visit France to look at a particular bloom.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flower' wants to be a bloom; it is the crossword's river, something that flows. 'There' points back to France, where the leave-taking is said in French.
annotation.definitionFit: A French farewell, used loosely: the phrase is what a speaker says on leaving, so 'I'm going' paraphrases its use rather than its literal 'until we see again'.

entries.clue: Cover length cloaked in shadow (8)

indicatorNotes.cloaked in: a cloak wraps round its wearer, so the length is wrapped inside the shadow

blocks.note: umbra is the dark central shadow, as in an eclipse
an ell is an old measure of length

annotation.surface: Some stretch of ground lies hidden in shade.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cover' could be a verb, but it is the noun: something held over you.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a rain shield is a cover, and the word also stretches to anything that protects or shelters, as in an umbrella organisation.

entries.clue: Earl possibly imputable — he is to suffer abasement (3,6,3)

indicatorNotes.possibly: the letters are one possible arrangement, so rearrange them

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for Earl

annotation.surface: A nobleman may be to blame, so he must accept humiliation.
annotation.walkthrough: The abbreviated Earl supplies the one extra E the rest of the fodder lacks.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'humble pie' was once umble pie, made from offal, food for servants, so eating it means accepting humiliation.

entries.clue: Recreational facility having dope in much supply (children excluded) (5,3)

indicatorNotes.supply: read as the adverb of supple: bendily, so rearrange
indicatorNotes.children excluded: CH, the abbreviation for children, is removed from 'much'

blocks.note: taken as it stands, before the deletion
CH = children; these letters are removed from MUCH, leaving MU for the anagram

annotation.surface: A leisure venue where drugs are plentiful, so no children allowed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supply' reads as the verb or noun; here it is the adverb from supple, flexibly.
annotation.definitionFit: A wry description: a den for smoking opium is a facility for recreational drug use, and the whole clue half-reads as its description.

entries.clue: Roué on vacation, getting his bit on the side? (4-3)

blocks.note: a roué is a debauched man, a rake

annotation.surface: A womaniser on holiday finds himself a mistress.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bit on the side' suggests an affair, which fits the roué, but here it is an illicit cut of money.
annotation.definitionFit: A slangy paraphrase: a rake-off is a share of profits skimmed, often dishonestly, so it is money on the side.

entries.clue: Weepy’s not tense — too much talk (6)

indicatorNotes.not: 'not tense' means without the tense, so the T is taken away

blocks.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense; it is removed

annotation.surface: A sentimental film that is not gripping, just endless chatter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Weepy' as a noun is a sad film, but it is needed as the adjective. 'Tense' is the grammatical T, not nervousness.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal noun: getting an earful means being subjected to a long stream of talk, usually a telling-off.

entries.clue: Slight noise made by consumer finishing early (4)

indicatorNotes.finishing early: the word stops one letter short, losing its last letter

blocks.note: the sound of someone eating or drinking noisily; its final P is dropped

annotation.surface: A small sound made by a shopper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Consumer' suggests a shopper, but it is someone eating or drinking. 'Slight' is a noun here, an insult, not an adjective meaning small.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the noun sense: both are insults, a slight snubbing someone and a slur casting aspersions on them.

entries.clue: Convict’s right, in the first instance, to give way to old potential killer (8)

indicatorNotes.in the first instance: only the first R is replaced
indicatorNotes.to give way to: the R steps aside for the O, as traffic gives way

blocks.note: R = right; the first R is removed
O = old; it takes the R's place

annotation.surface: A prisoner's legal right must yield to that of an old man who could be dangerous.
annotation.walkthrough: PRISONER has two Rs; 'in the first instance' says only the first changes.
annotation.definitionFit: A description with a hedge: someone who administers poison may or may not succeed, so 'potential killer' is fair.

entries.clue: Active California couple endlessly dancing in city (8)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: the last letter of 'couple' is dropped
indicatorNotes.dancing: the remaining letters move about into a new order

blocks.note: the word without its end, rearranged

annotation.surface: A lively Californian pair dancing nonstop somewhere in town.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface places the couple in a city; that last word is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the answer is a resort city on Mexico's Pacific coast.

entries.clue: Help or, for one paying attention, insight (4)

indicatorNotes.for one paying attention: a listener hears the word rather than reading it

blocks.note: a plain synonym, usually of helping in wrongdoing
heard rather than read, this is a word meaning to urge on

annotation.walkthrough: The second definition only works by ear: 'insight' sounds like 'incite', which does mean to egg on, as the answer does.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are encouragement: to help someone, especially in crime, and to incite, the word that 'insight' sounds like.

entries.clue: Fraud chooses to run inherently unstable scheme (5,2,5)

indicatorNotes.to run: the letters run about into a new order

annotation.surface: A con artist elects to set up a shaky money-making plan.
annotation.walkthrough: The fraud surface fits the answer, which is why the anagram hides so well.
annotation.definitionFit: A metaphor: a tower of playing cards falls at a touch, so the phrase names any flimsy plan bound to collapse.

entries.clue: Naked woman, finding clergyman on couch (minus head), ran (12)

indicatorNotes.Naked: the woman is stripped of her outer letters, as of her clothes
indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, one piece sits on top of the next
indicatorNotes.minus head: the couch loses its first letter

blocks.note: LADY with its outer letters stripped

annotation.surface: A woman with no clothes fled on finding a vicar on her sofa.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ran' looks like fled, but it is ran as in managed.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the managerial sense: you run or administer a business, a department or an estate.

entries.clue: Strike hard to break plot Trump’s damned (6)

indicatorNotes.to break: the first word breaks into the second, splitting it

blocks.note: a plot of garden, a flower bed

annotation.surface: A political outburst about a scheme being ruined.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trump's' marks the definition as American: the word is heard in US speech as a mild oath.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional euphemism: Americans say 'the blamed thing won't start' where others would curse, so Trump's word stands for damned.

entries.clue: Doctor’s charging not restrained? That’s a regular occurrence (4,4)

indicatorNotes.charging: the doctor charges into the middle of the phrase

annotation.surface: A doctor's fees have no limit, and that happens all the time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Charging' suggests fees; it means rushing in. The ''s' is 'is', making the doctor the one charging.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the moon is full roughly every 29 and a half days, so it is literally a regular occurrence.

entries.clue: Trail in Glamorgan goes round fencing (7)

indicatorNotes.goes round: the outer words go round the answer, enclosing it

blocks.note: the letters sit inside these three words, from the second letter of 'Trail' to the G of 'Glamorgan'

annotation.surface: A footpath in a Welsh county loops about.
annotation.walkthrough: Glamorgan is a county in south Wales. The trail's first letter and the county's tail wrap round the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a row of rails is fencing, as round a park.

entries.clue: Keeper from Orient regularly put off by opposing players breaking into song (8)

indicatorNotes.put off by: the first piece is set off, leading the rest
indicatorNotes.breaking into: the players break into the song

blocks.note: North and East, opponents at bridge

annotation.surface: A goalkeeper from Leyton Orient is upset by the other side bursting into a chant.
annotation.walkthrough: Leyton Orient is a London football club, so 'Keeper' reads as a goalie. At bridge, North partners South, so North and East are on opposite sides.
annotation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned sense: a retainer is a long-serving servant, one who keeps a household or is kept on by it.

entries.clue: One making allowance for soldiers led by Ulysses? (7)

indicatorNotes.led by: the soldiers come after the leader

blocks.note: Ulysses S. Grant, Union general and US president

annotation.surface: Troops under Ulysses are cut some slack.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ulysses' suggests the Greek hero, but it is General Grant.
annotation.definitionFit: A legal term: the grantor is the party who grants, allowing or conveying something to another.

entries.clue: Memorial probed by local government type (8)

indicatorNotes.probed by: the local pokes into the memorial

blocks.note: a relic is a keepsake or memorial
your local is your nearest pub

annotation.surface: A war memorial being investigated by a council official.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Local government' reads as a unit; split it, and 'local' is the pub.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: rule by elected representatives with no monarch is one kind of government.

entries.clue: Latte reportedly served up part way through light entertainment (8)

indicatorNotes.served up: in a down clue, up runs the letters backwards
indicatorNotes.part way through: the answer lies partly within the words

annotation.surface: A coffee, it is said, was brought midway through a show.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reportedly' is not a homophone signal here; it just contributes letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by genre: a little opera with spoken dialogue and a comic plot is light musical entertainment.

entries.clue: Gullible American lawyer taking off east, lands in Caribbean (7)

indicatorNotes.taking off: to take something off is to remove it, so one E goes

blocks.note: E = east, the letter taken off GREEN
a district attorney, a US prosecutor

annotation.surface: A naive US attorney flies out eastwards and touches down in the West Indies.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lands' reads as a verb; it is the plural noun, the territory of an island state.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by location: the answer is an island nation, its lands lying in the southern Caribbean.

entries.clue: Crosspiece held back cover for opening (8)

blocks.note: split into cross = ROOD (a crucifix) and piece = PART

annotation.surface: A timber beam kept behind a hatch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crosspiece' reads as one word, a beam; split it into cross and piece.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: a hinged flap set flush in a floor or ceiling covers an opening.

entries.clue: Alloy of gold and molybdenum initially lacking use (6)

indicatorNotes.initially: take the first letters of the next words

blocks.note: first letters of lacking and use

annotation.surface: A metal mixture of gold and molybdenum that turns out to be useless.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is almost literal, since the answer is a gold-coloured metal.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: gilded bronze, or a gold-coloured mix of copper, zinc and tin, used on furniture.

entries.clue: House in bits, trail of debris covering central source of explosion (6)

indicatorNotes.covering: the S covers up the E, taking its place
indicatorNotes.central: the E to replace is the one in the middle of the word

blocks.note: the first letter of explosion; the middle E of PIECES is the one replaced

annotation.surface: A home blown to pieces, rubble strewn across the heart of the blast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'House' is astrological: each sign of the zodiac is a house.
annotation.definitionFit: An astrological sense: the twelve zodiac signs are called houses, and the Fish is the last of them.

entries.clue: Seemingly endless output from Bernini working with metal (12)

indicatorNotes.working: the letters are worked into a new shape

annotation.surface: The Baroque sculptor Bernini turning out bronzes without pause.
annotation.walkthrough: Bernini was the great Italian Baroque sculptor, which makes 'working with metal' a natural picture.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with a hedge: the word means having no end, used of things that only feel endless, like a meeting.

entries.clue: Equestrian gear in bad taste (4)

blocks.note: saddles, bridles and harness, short for tackle
an old dialect noun for an unpleasant flavour or tang

annotation.surface: Riding kit that is vulgar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bad taste' suggests tacky, but the second sense is an old word for an off flavour.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: horse gear, from tackle; and a dialect word, still in Chambers, for a disagreeable lingering taste.

entries.clue: Book on sport’s extremely thorough (4)

indicatorNotes.extremely: take the extremes, the first and last letters

annotation.surface: A sports book is very comprehensive.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Book' is a book of the Bible.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: one of the books of the Old Testament, named after its heroine.

entries.clue: Out of prison, journalist was exceptionally good (8)

blocks.note: ex = out of, from, as in ex works
a cell is a prison room

annotation.surface: A reporter, freed from jail, did outstanding work.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma splits a story about a released reporter into three pieces and a definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: to stand out above others is to be exceptionally good.

entries.clue: Rustic Scots islander gets acre for nothing (8)

indicatorNotes.gets: the islander takes on something new
indicatorNotes.for: the A stands in for the O

blocks.note: O looks like zero; it is replaced

annotation.surface: A farmer from the Scottish islands acquires land for free.
annotation.walkthrough: Orkney is an island group off northern Scotland; its people are Orcadians.
annotation.definitionFit: A literary sense: Arcadia, a Greek region, became the poets' ideal of simple country life, so the adjective means idyllically rustic.
